item.description:
America 250 Speaker Series Honoring the Stories. Understanding Our History.
Join the AAHGS North Carolina Triangle Chapter for our America 250 Speaker Series, a four-part virtual educational program highlighting the lives, service, contributions, and legacies of African Americans and other People of Color whose stories have often been overlooked in traditional historical narratives.
As our nation commemorates the 250th anniversary of the United States, this series brings together respected genealogists, historians, researchers, and educators to explore Revolutionary War history, family history, local history, and lineage research through a broader and more inclusive lens.

item.title: Centennial Sounds — Mon Sep 14, 7:00 PM — Folk School Festival Barn
item.description:
Amplifying diverse Appalachian voices
Music and dance have been a vital part of the Folk School since its founding in 1925. As we celebrate our 100th year, Centennial Sounds honors this legacy by spotlighting the cultural richness of Appalachian music and the many voices that shape it. This special performance series will feature five headliners whose work expands and redefines the story of Appalachian music. Through these concerts, we aim to create new opportunities for our community in Western North Carolina to experience the full spectrum of Appalachian sound.
The Folk School is supported by the North Carolina Arts Council, a division of the Department of Natural and Cultural Resources.

item.title: Ackland Film Forum: "Z" (Costa-Gavras, 1969) — Mon Sep 14, 7:30 PM — The Lumina Theater
item.description:
Yves Montand, Jean-Louis Trintignant, and Irène Papas headline this electrifying political thriller. A politician is assassinated in broad daylight, setting in motion an investigation that gradually exposes the distance between official narratives and lived reality. Racing ahead with remarkable urgency, Z channels late-1960s anti-authoritarian currents and the growing sense that democratic institutions can no longer be taken at face value. This film will be introduced by Professor Henry Veggian, UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature. It will be screened at 7:30 p.m. at The Lumina Theater (620 Market St, Chapel Hill, NC 27516). Tickets are free for all audience members, and registration is required via The Lumina’s webpage. When this link is live, click to reserve your free ticket. UNC-Chapel Hill students can receive CLE credit for attending by scanning the QR code at the event.

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Tue Sep 15 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words — Tue Sep 15 — Welborn Gallery
item.description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026
This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

item.title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence — Tue Sep 15, 10:00 AM — Kings Mountain Historical Museum
item.description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.
The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Tue Sep 15, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: TENDING | Black Farmers Fight for Justice Against the USDA — Tue Sep 15, 10:00 AM — None
item.description:
Shirlette Ammons shares her thought process on developing* *TENDING*** ***Black Farmers Fight for Justice Against the USDA (an audio documentary)
Ammons is a poet, storyteller, and musician, but most importantly, the granddaughter of a Black farmer.
Ammons traveled across 7 states, including my native North Carolina. Roamed the fields & farmland, sat on the porches, and ate at the dinner tables of some of the tens of thousands of Black farmers across the country who were claimants in Pigford vs Glickman, once the largest class action lawsuit in US history.
The question about this audio documentary:
Why has the United States, its federal and its local governments, worked so strategically to keep Black people from owning and stewarding land?

item.title: FIP Seminar: Non-destructive 3D pathology and analysis for optimizing treatments — Wed Sep 16, 12:00 PM — Wilkinson Building
item.description: We are developing non-destructive slide-free 3D pathology methods for clinical decision support and surgical guidance. In comparison to conventional slide-based pathology, 3D pathology provides: (1) vastly greater sampling of tissue specimens including whole biopsies and surgical margins, (2) volumetric imaging of cell distributions and 3D tissue structures that are prognostic and predictive, and (3) a non-destructive and reversible workflow that preserves valuable specimens for downstream molecular assays. Due to the immense size of feature-rich 3D pathology datasets, new challenges exist in terms of data management, human visualization, and computer-aided interpretation. Participants gather to ring bells, much as the church bells of Philadelphia rang out when the U.S. Constitution was first signed at 4 pm on September 17, 1787. Hayes, author of Schools of Our Own: Chicago’s Golden Age of Black Private Education and a coming biography of Doris Allen Anderson, will lead this conversation. Attendees are welcome to bring in samples of mushrooms from their own property. Place any samples in a paper bag, and do not eat any mushrooms found, as they may be poisonous.
The hike will begin from the Linville Gorge Overlook parking lot, which is just inside the Paddy's Creek Access's entrance gate on the right.
Please note: collecting mushrooms is prohibited in North Carolina State Parks. There will be no foray as part of this program.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Luminary & Freedom Stories — Fri Sep 18, 7:00 PM — Bennett Place State Historic Site
item.description:
During this special luminary program, Bennett Place invites you to reflect on the end of the Civil War as a momentous step towards freedom for all Americans and the end of chattel slavery in the United States.
Walk among 3,310 luminaries - one for every 1,000 enslaved people in North Carolina - and reflect on experiences of enslavement and freedom. Historians dot the path and share stories of people's pathways to freedom and life after slavery & the Civil War.
---
Harriet Ann Daves recalled just how monumental Civil War surrenders were for her family: "When the surrender came my grandfather came to my mother and told her: 'Well, you are as free as I am.'"
Claiming freedom was not so straightforward for the 331,059 enslaved women, children, and men in North Carolina during the Civil War. Some took enormous risk to reach Union lines before the federal government made any promise of abolishing slavery. Others left their homes and plantations to follow Sherman's army as they marched
